original_value: AbstractMalaria is a tropical parasitic disease caused by the Plasmodium genus, which resulted in an estimated 219 million cases of malaria and 435 000 malaria-related deaths in 2017. Despite the availability of the Plasmodium falciparum genome since 2002, 74% of the genes remain uncharacterized. To remedy this paucity of functional information, we used transcriptomic data to build gene co-expression networks for two Plasmodium species (P. falciparum and P. berghei), and included genomic data of four other Plasmodium species, P. yoelii, P. knowlesi, P. vivax and P. cynomolgi, as well as two non-Plasmodium species from the Apicomplexa, Toxoplasma gondii and Theileria parva. The genomic and transcriptomic data were incorporated into the resulting database, malaria.tools, which is preloaded with tools that allow the identification and cross-species comparison of co-expressed gene neighbourhoods, clusters and life stage-specific expression, thus providing sophisticated tools to predict gene function. Moreover, we exemplify how the tools can be used to easily identify genes relevant for pathogenicity and various life stages of the malaria parasite. The database is freely available at www.malaria.tools.

result.paraphrase: Malaria is a tropical parasitic disease caused by Plasmodium, which led to an estimated 219 million cases and 435,000 malaria-related deaths in 2017. Although the Plasmodium falciparum genome has been available since 2002, 74% of its genes remain uncharacterized. To address this lack of functional information, we used transcriptomic data to construct gene co-expression networks for two Plasmodium species, P. falciparum and P. berghei, and incorporated genomic data from four additional Plasmodium species, P. yoelii, P. knowlesi, P. vivax and P. cynomolgi, plus two non-Plasmodium apicomplexans, Toxoplasma gondii and Theileria parva. These genomic and transcriptomic datasets were integrated into the malaria.tools database, which comes preloaded with tools for identifying and comparing co-expressed gene neighborhoods, clusters, and life stage-specific expression across species, thereby offering advanced tools for predicting gene function. We also show how these tools can be used to readily identify genes linked to pathogenicity and different life stages of the malaria parasite. The database is freely accessible at www.malaria.tools.
